solution.concept_anchor: Simple majority amendments excluded from Article 368
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students conflate 'changing constitutional text' with 'amendment under Article 368,' assuming any textual alteration to the Constitution must use the special procedure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 368 governs amendments to the Constitution requiring special majority — but several provisions explicitly permit Parliament to act by ordinary law, bypassing Article 368 entirely.

Eliminate (c): Presidential assent under Article 368 applies to amendments processed through that article; simple majority amendments are ordinary legislation and do not follow the Article 368 procedure.

Eliminate (d): The Basic Structure doctrine as articulated in Kesavananda Bharati applies to amendments made under Article 368 — its applicability to simple majority provisions operating outside Article 368 is debated, making (d) an overstatement.

Select (b): Because simple majority provisions are explicitly authorised by individual articles (e.g., Article 11, 169, 3) and are treated as ordinary legislation, they are wholly outside the Article 368 procedure.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the common student assumption that any change to the text of the Constitution must go through Article 368. In fact, several constitutional provisions themselves authorise Parliament to act 'by law' — which means ordinary legislation by simple majority. These do not constitute 'amendments' in the Article 368 sense, do not require Presidential assent under the Article 368 procedure, and do not need to satisfy the special majority or ratification conditions. A partially prepared student will instinctively mark (a) or (c), anchored to the idea that constitutionally significant changes must use the formal amendment route.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Constitution distinguishes between two types of changes to its content: amendments under Article 368 (requiring special majority and sometimes state ratification) and changes authorised by individual articles through ordinary legislation (simple majority). The latter are not governed by Article 368 at all.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Not every change to the constitutional text requires Article 368. Several articles explicitly authorise Parliament to act 'by law,' making the change through ordinary legislation.
• Option (b) — Correct: Simple majority amendments operate through provisions in individual articles that grant Parliament legislative power. They bypass Article 368 entirely and are treated as ordinary legislation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Presidential assent under Article 368(2) applies only to Bills processed through that article. Simple majority laws receive Presidential assent as ordinary Bills, not under the Article 368 procedure.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Basic Structure doctrine's applicability to simple majority provisions outside Article 368 is contested — this option overstates settled law.

Value Addition:
• Article 368 itself does not define 'amendment' to cover all constitutional changes — only those explicitly routed through it.
• Examples: Articles 2, 3, 11, 169, 312 all use the phrase 'by law' or 'by legislation' signalling simple majority.
• The Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973) applied Basic Structure to Article 368 amendments — its reach to simple majority provisions remains jurisprudentially open.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 169 — asymmetric majority for Legislative Council

statement_analysis.statement: For Parliament to create or abolish a State Legislative Council under Article 169, it needs to pass the enabling legislation by a special majority.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 169, once the State Assembly passes a resolution by special majority, Parliament enacts the legislation by simple majority — Parliament does NOT need a special majority.

statement_analysis.statement: Before Parliament can act under Article 169, the State Legislative Assembly must pass a resolution expressing its desire by a majority of its total membership and not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 169(1) expressly requires the State Assembly to pass a resolution by an absolute majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting before Parliament can legislate.

statement_analysis.statement: A law made under Article 169 is not deemed a constitutional amendment for the purposes of Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 169(3) explicitly states that such a law shall not be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368, though it alters a constitutional provision.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who correctly know that 'special majority' is involved in Article 169 conflate Parliament's role with the State Assembly's role, assuming both houses/bodies need special majority.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Parliament requires only simple majority under Article 169 — the special majority burden falls on the State Assembly, not Parliament. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 169(1) mandates the State Assembly resolution by total majority + 2/3 of members present and voting — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 169(3) explicitly excludes such laws from the definition of 'amendment' under Article 368 — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The signature trap in Article 169 questions is the asymmetric majority requirement. Students who know 'special majority is involved' invariably apply it to Parliament rather than (or in addition to) the State Assembly. In reality, Parliament passes the law by simple majority — it is the State Assembly that must achieve special majority. Further, Article 169(3)'s explicit exclusion from Article 368 is a highly testable provision that most students overlook.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 169 provides a unique procedure for creating or abolishing State Legislative Councils. The process has two stages with different majority thresholds applied to different bodies.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Parliament legislates under Article 169 by simple majority. The special majority requirement applies exclusively to the State Legislative Assembly's resolution, not to Parliament's vote.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The State Assembly must pass a resolution by (i) a majority of its total membership and (ii) not less than two-thirds of members present and voting — a double-lock special majority.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 169(3) explicitly provides that such legislation shall not be deemed an amendment for Article 368 purposes, even though it alters a constitutional provision about the state's legislature.

Value Addition:
• Recent examples: Andhra Pradesh's Legislative Council was abolished and later reconstituted; J&K's Council was abolished when the state was reorganised in 2019.
• The State Assembly's resolution is not binding on Parliament — Parliament may decline to pass the law.
• This is one of the clearest examples where a change to constitutional structure occurs outside Article 368.

solution.concept_anchor: Fifth vs Sixth Schedule amendment procedures

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) and the Sixth Schedule (Tribal Areas in Northeast) can be amended by Parliament through ordinary legislation by simple majority.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Schedules are amenable to simple majority legislation by Parliament — the Sixth Schedule, despite its complexity, does not require the Article 368 special majority procedure for amendment by Parliament.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sixth Schedule applies to tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Arunachal Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sixth Schedule applies to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram — not Arunachal Pradesh. Arunachal Pradesh is covered under the Fifth Schedule framework.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Fifth Schedule, the President (not the State Governor) has the power to increase or decrease Scheduled Areas by order.
statement_analysis.reason: Para 6 of the Fifth Schedule vests the power to increase or diminish Scheduled Areas, and to alter their boundaries, in the President by public notification.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students familiar with Sixth Schedule's complex governance structure assume it must require a higher amendment threshold, when it does not.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Both Fifth and Sixth Schedules are amendable by Parliament through simple majority — this is correct, so Statement 1 is NOT incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — Arunachal Pradesh is NOT in this list. Statement 2 is factually incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Fifth Schedule Para 6 vests power to alter Scheduled Areas in the President — this is correct, so Statement 3 is NOT incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits two common conflations: (i) the assumption that the Sixth Schedule's elaborate governance structure necessitates a higher amendment threshold, and (ii) the geographic confusion between Arunachal Pradesh (Fifth Schedule state) and Mizoram (Sixth Schedule state). Students who have memorised the northeastern states as a block will often swap Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh in Sixth Schedule questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Fifth and Sixth Schedules address tribal governance but apply to different regions and through different institutional frameworks.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Parliament can amend both Schedules by simple majority. Neither Schedule requires Article 368 procedure for amendment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. Arunachal Pradesh is NOT covered under the Sixth Schedule; it falls under the general Fifth Schedule framework.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The President holds the power under Fifth Schedule Para 6 to modify Scheduled Area boundaries by notification.

Value Addition:
• The Sixth Schedule provides for Autonomous District Councils with quasi-legislative and judicial powers.
• PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas with tribal-sensitive modifications — it is ordinary legislation (simple majority).
• Mizoram's inclusion in the Sixth Schedule reflects the Mizo Accord of 1986 — a frequently tested connection.
• Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, and Manipur (hill areas) have special provisions under Article 371 series, not Sixth Schedule.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 3 — Parliament's powers over states and territories

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament may, by simple majority, increase the area of any existing State.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3(b) empowers Parliament to increase the area of any State through ordinary legislation by simple majority.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 3, Parliament is bound to act in accordance with the opinion expressed by the State Legislature when reorganising state boundaries.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires Parliament to refer the Bill to the concerned State Legislature for its opinion, but Parliament is NOT bound by that opinion and can proceed regardless.

statement_analysis.statement: Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised into two Union Territories in 2019 through ordinary legislation passed by simple majority.
statement_analysis.reason: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019 was passed by simple majority, using Parliament's plenary power over Union Territories under Article 3 read with the First Schedule.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament's power under Article 3 to alter state boundaries requires the prior consent of the affected State Legislature before introducing the Bill.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires only the President to refer the Bill to the State Legislature for its opinion within a specified time — prior consent of the state is not required. The Bill can be introduced without the state's agreement.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who know 'state opinion is required' conflate the opinion requirement with a consent or binding requirement, leading them to mark both Statements 2 and 4 as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 3(b) explicitly grants Parliament this power — correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Parliament must seek the State Legislature's opinion but is not bound by it — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 was ordinary legislation — correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Article 3 requires Presidential reference for opinion, not prior state consent — Statement 4 is incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statements 2 and 4 together exploit the most common confusion about Article 3: the difference between seeking an opinion and obtaining consent. Many students know that the state legislature must be consulted and incorrectly infer that Parliament must follow that opinion or obtain prior consent. Article 3 is a deliberate assertion of parliamentary supremacy over federal units — India's 'indestructible Union' principle.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 3 is among the most powerful provisions affirming parliamentary supremacy in India's federal structure. It grants Parliament sweeping authority to reshape states and territories by simple majority.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 3(b) explicitly includes increasing a state's area as one of Parliament's powers.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Parliament is required to refer the Bill to the State Legislature for its opinion (within a Presidential-set timeline), but is not bound to follow that opinion.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019, which bifurcated the erstwhile state into two UTs (J&K and Ladakh), was passed by simple majority — a landmark exercise of this power.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The state's prior consent is not a constitutional prerequisite. Only a reference for opinion is required, and even that is through the President's direction, not a direct state-Parliament negotiation.

Value Addition:
• India is described as an 'indestructible Union of destructible States' — contrasted with the USA where state boundaries cannot be altered without state consent.
• Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not deemed constitutional amendments under Article 368.
• Telangana's creation in 2014 from Andhra Pradesh is the most recent Article 3 example before J&K's reorganisation.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 312 two-step process for All-India Services
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students who know Article 312 involves Rajya Sabha and a 2/3 majority conflate the Rajya Sabha resolution threshold with the parliamentary legislation threshold, placing both under 'special majority.'
elimination_logic: Match A: Article 312 requires Rajya Sabha to pass a resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting — then Parliament creates the service by ordinary law. A matches with 3.
Match B: Article 118 authorises Parliament to make rules of procedure by simple majority — B matches with 1.
Match C: Article 100 sets quorum at 1/10th of total membership for each House — C matches with 4.
Match D: Article 169 requires the State Assembly to pass a resolution by special majority (not Parliament) — D matches with 2.
Correct combination: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap for item A (Article 312) is the two-step majority confusion: the Rajya Sabha resolution requires 2/3 majority (a form of special majority), but the actual legislation creating the service is simple majority. Options (b) and (c) exploit this by pairing A with incorrect descriptions. Item D (Article 169) adds a second trap: the special majority is needed from the State Assembly, not Parliament — students who know 'special majority is involved' may incorrectly associate it with Parliament's role.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of how different constitutional provisions assign different majority thresholds to different bodies in a multi-step process.

**Correct Matches:**
• A (Article 312) — 3: The Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting declaring a new All-India Service necessary; Parliament then enacts the legislation by simple majority. No new All-India Service has been created since the Indian Forest Service in 1966.
• B (Article 118) — 1: Parliament makes its own rules of procedure by simple majority. These procedural rules do not require Article 368 procedure.
• C (Article 100) — 4: The quorum required in each House is 1/10th of its total membership. This threshold can be changed by ordinary law.
• D (Article 169) — 2: The State Legislative Assembly must pass a resolution by special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting). Parliament's own vote on the legislation is by simple majority.

Value Addition:
• Article 312(3): Parliament can create All-India Services common to the Union and States.
• The Anti-Defection provisions in the Tenth Schedule require Article 368 special majority to amend — contrasting sharply with ordinary parliamentary procedural rules.
• Federal safeguard in Article 312: The Rajya Sabha, representing states, must initiate the creation of a new All-India Service — a rare instance of the Upper House having exclusive initiating power.

upsc_trap_explanation: The trap for item A (Article 312) is the two-step majority confusion: the Rajya Sabha resolution requires 2/3 majority, but the actual legislation creating the service needs only simple majority. Students often conflate these two steps and apply the higher threshold to the wrong stage. Item D compounds this by involving a special majority from the State Assembly — not Parliament — which students routinely mis-attribute.

solution.concept_anchor: Delimitation history and 91st Amendment freeze
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) traps students who know the 91st Amendment is related to delimitation but do not know the correct sequence relative to the Delimitation Act 2002.
elimination_logic: The first Delimitation Commission was established under the Delimitation Commission Act 1952 — this is the earliest event.
The Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act 1976 froze delimitation following the 1971 census — this comes after the first Commission but before the 2002 Act.
The Delimitation Act 2002 re-established the Commission for the 2001 census-based delimitation — after the 1976 freeze was partially lifted.

The Constitution (84th Amendment) Act 2001 and (87th Amendment) Act 2003 extended the freeze and adjusted seat allocation — the 91st Amendment (2003) dealt with defection, not delimitation directly. The freeze until 2026 was by the 84th Amendment. Sequence: 1952 Commission → 1976 freeze (42nd Amendment) → 2002 Delimitation Act → 84th Amendment freeze extension.
Correct chronological order: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2 — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students confuse the 42nd Amendment's delimitation freeze (1976) with the 84th Amendment's extension (2001). Both involve freezing seat delimitation, but at different census benchmarks and for different durations. The Delimitation Act 2002's position in the sequence — after the freeze but enabling boundary readjustment — is the specific knowledge gap this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
Delimitation — redrawing constituency boundaries based on census data — has had a turbulent legislative history in India.

**Correct sequence:**
1. **Delimitation Commission Act, 1952** — The first statutory Delimitation Commission was established after the first general elections to conduct seat allocation based on the 1951 census.
2. **42nd Amendment Act, 1976** — Froze the number of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats based on the 1971 census until the first census after 2000, suspending fresh delimitation.
3. **Delimitation Act, 2002** — Re-established a Delimitation Commission for readjusting constituency boundaries (not seat numbers) based on the 2001 census data.
4. **84th Amendment Act, 2001** — Extended the freeze on total seat numbers until the first census after 2026, though boundary readjustment within existing seats was permitted.

**Wrong options eliminated:** Options placing 1976 (42nd Amendment) after the 2002 Act, or placing the 84th Amendment before the first Delimitation Commission, reflect common temporal confusions.

Value Addition:
• The Delimitation Commission's orders have the force of law under Article 82 and cannot be challenged in any court.
• The freeze until 2026 has significant political implications — states that controlled population growth are penalised in seat allocation.
• Delimitation Commission is a statutory (not constitutional) body — created by Parliament by simple majority.

solution.concept_anchor: Parliament's plenary power over Union Territories
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) traps students who know 'constitutional amendment is required to alter territory' and assume Article 368 special majority applies, not recognising that UTs are altered through ordinary legislation under Article 3 read with the First Schedule.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves Parliament merging two existing Union Territories — this falls squarely within Parliament's power under Article 3 read with the First Schedule.
Union Territories are not 'states' — Parliament has plenary power over them without the Article 3 requirement of Presidential reference to a State Legislature (which applies only to states).
Creating, modifying, or abolishing UTs is done through ordinary legislation by simple majority — Article 368 is not required. Eliminate option (b).
The consent of the UT's legislature (if it has one) is not constitutionally required — Parliament acts unilaterally. Eliminate options (c) and (d).
Select option (a): Parliament may enact the merger legislation by simple majority without the constraints applicable to reorganisation of States.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits students' tendency to apply the Article 3 procedure (Presidential reference to State Legislature) to Union Territories as well as states. The Article 3 reference requirement applies specifically to the concerned State Legislature — UTs either have no legislature or their legislatures do not have the same constitutional standing. Parliament's power over UTs is near-absolute and exercisable through simple majority legislation, as demonstrated by the J&K Reorganisation Act 2019.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliament's authority over Union Territories is qualitatively different from its authority over States under Article 3. While reorganising States requires Presidential reference to the concerned State Legislature (though not binding), no such procedural requirement exists for modifying Union Territories.

**Applicable principle:** Parliament may create, modify, or abolish Union Territories through ordinary legislation by simple majority, using its power under Article 3 read with the First Schedule. Article 368's special majority is not required.

**Applying to the scenario:** The proposed merger of two UTs is a modification of the First Schedule (list of Union Territories). Parliament can do this by passing an ordinary Bill by simple majority in both Houses, followed by Presidential assent as ordinary legislation.

• Option (a) — Correct: Simple majority suffices; no special majority or state consultation required.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 368 special majority is not required for UT reorganisation — this was settled by the J&K Reorganisation Act 2019.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The UT's legislature (if any) need not concur — Parliament has plenary power over UTs.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No ratification by state legislatures is needed.

Value Addition:
• Ladakh was carved out as a UT without a legislature in 2019 — both Ladakh (no legislature) and J&K (with legislature) created by simple majority.
• Parliament is the legislature for all UTs without their own legislature under Article 239A.
• Puducherry and Delhi have partial statehood — but their creation/modification still rests with Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: Second Schedule — charged vs votable salary provisions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students know judges' salaries are 'special' (charged to Consolidated Fund) and assume this makes the Schedule provision also specially protected, when in fact the Schedule amounts can be changed by simple majority.
elimination_logic: Identify the shared attribute: options (a), (b), (c) all involve constitutional functionaries whose emoluments are listed in the Second Schedule and are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable by Parliament).

Check option (d): MPs' salaries are determined by Parliament 'by law' under Article 106 — they are NOT listed in the Second Schedule and are NOT charged to the Consolidated Fund. MPs' salaries are voted on by Parliament through ordinary legislation.
The odd one out is option (d) — MPs' salaries fall outside the Second Schedule framework entirely.
Select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in the assumption that all senior constitutional functionaries' salaries are covered under the Second Schedule. MPs are powerful constitutional actors but their remuneration is a matter of ordinary law (Article 106), not Schedule protection — creating an important asymmetry that this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Schedule of the Constitution specifies emoluments for certain high constitutional offices. These emoluments are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India, meaning they are non-votable — Parliament cannot reduce them through the annual budget process.

• Option (a) — Comptroller and Auditor General: Covered in Second Schedule (Part E). CAG's salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund.
• Option (b) — Judges of the Supreme Court: Covered in Second Schedule (Part D). Their salaries are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.
• Option (c) — Governors of States: Covered in Second Schedule (Part B). Governors' emoluments are charged to the Consolidated Fund of the State.
• Option (d) — Members of Parliament: NOT in the Second Schedule. MPs' salaries and allowances are determined by Parliament itself through ordinary legislation under Article 106. This is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• The Second Schedule also covers the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
• Judges' salaries cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment — a judicial independence safeguard.
• Parliament periodically revises MPs' salaries through the Salaries, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954 — amendable by simple majority.

solution.concept_anchor: 100th Amendment — special majority for First Schedule alteration

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution (100th Amendment) Act 2015, which implemented the Land Boundary Agreement between India and Bangladesh, was passed by Parliament through a simple majority as it involved only an administrative territorial adjustment within existing Indian territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The 100th Amendment Act 2015 required Article 368 procedure — special majority in both Houses plus ratification by at least half the State Legislatures — because it altered the First Schedule of the Constitution by modifying territorial descriptions. It was not a simple majority measure.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Constitution, Parliament's power to make administrative changes within existing Union Territory boundaries does not require the Article 368 special majority procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament's authority over Union Territories is exercisable through ordinary legislation (simple majority); only changes that alter the First Schedule entries or affect State territories in the manner triggering Article 368 require the special majority procedure.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know the 100th Amendment involved 'territory' may conflate 'territorial change' with 'simple majority administrative action,' assuming the Bangladesh land swap was routine.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 100th Amendment altered the First Schedule — this requires Article 368 special majority AND state ratification. The Amendment was NOT passed by simple majority. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Administrative changes within existing UT boundaries do not require Article 368 — this is constitutionally accurate. Statement 2 is correct.
Pattern: Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the implicit assumption that since India 'gained' territory through the Bangladesh land boundary agreement, it must have been a simple executive/legislative act. In fact, because the agreement involved India ceding enclaves to Bangladesh and receiving others — thereby altering the territorial description in the First Schedule — it required Article 368 procedure with state ratification. This distinguishes 'adding to the First Schedule' (special majority) from 'administrative changes within existing territory' (simple majority).
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution's First Schedule lists the territories of India. Any alteration to this Schedule — whether adding or removing territory — triggers Article 368 requirements.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 100th Amendment Act 2015 was passed using Article 368 procedure: special majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures. The Agreement involved exchange of enclaves with Bangladesh, changing the First Schedule's territorial description — this is not a routine administrative action.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Parliament's powers over Union Territories and administrative reorganisation within existing territorial boundaries operate through ordinary legislation. The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 (simple majority) is a textbook example.

Value Addition:
• The 100th Amendment transferred 111 Indian enclaves to Bangladesh and received 51 Bangladeshi enclaves — a net territorial exchange.
• It required state ratification because it affected the First Schedule — one of the schedules whose alteration triggers the ratification requirement under Article 368.
• Territory cession (giving up territory) vs territory acquisition (gaining territory) — both require constitutional amendment if the First Schedule is affected.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

solution.concept_anchor: Article 138 — Parliament expands but cannot curtail SC jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) misleads students who know Parliament has power over the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and assume this includes the power to curtail it through ordinary legislation.
elimination_logic: Article 138 allows Parliament to extend the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and powers through ordinary legislation — simple majority.
However, Parliament cannot curtail the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction (original, appellate) by simple majority — that would require constitutional amendment.
The blank describes what Parliament CAN do under Article 138 — extend, not curtail.
Select option (b): Parliament may by law extend the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter in the Union List.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Article 138's one-directional nature — expand, not curtail — is the core trap. Students assume symmetry: if Parliament can expand, it can also curtail. Constitutional jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is protected from ordinary legislative curtailment.
solution.final_explanation:

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliament cannot abolish the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction (Article 131) by ordinary law — that would require Article 368.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 138 empowers Parliament to extend the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter in the Union List by ordinary legislation (simple majority).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Parliament cannot curtail the Supreme Court's constitutionally guaranteed jurisdiction (Articles 131–136) by simple majority legislation.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Parliamentary oversight of SC judgments is not within Article 138's scope — judicial decisions are final subject to the Court's own review power.

Value Addition:

• Article 139 separately allows Parliament to confer power on the SC to issue writs for purposes other than those in Article 32.
• Article 140 allows Parliament to confer ancillary powers on the SC — all by simple majority.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 2 vs Article 3 — new vs existing state distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Article 2 enables Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, territories that are not already part of India, and this power is exercisable through ordinary legislation by simple majority.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 2 explicitly empowers Parliament to admit new states or establish new states on terms it thinks fit — through ordinary law, not Article 368. Sikkim's admission in 1975 initially used this route.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Article 3, Article 2 does not require the President to refer the proposed legislation to the concerned State Legislature before introducing it in Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The Presidential reference requirement (for seeking State Legislature's opinion) is specific to Article 3, which deals with existing states. Article 2 concerns new territories not yet part of India, so no existing state legislature is consulted.

statement_analysis.statement: The formation of new states under Article 3 out of existing Indian territory requires the consent of the affected State Legislature as a precondition for Parliament to introduce the Bill.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires only the President to refer the Bill to the concerned State Legislature for its opinion within a specified period. The state's consent is not required — Parliament can proceed regardless of the state's view.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) misleads students who know 'state opinion must be taken' and wrongly extend this to mean state consent is mandatory, marking Statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish new states by simple majority — correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Presidential reference to State Legislature is a requirement under Article 3 only — Article 2 territories are not part of India, so no state legislature is consulted. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 3 requires the President to seek the State Legislature's opinion, not its consent. Parliament is not bound by the opinion. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap: the word 'consent' replaces the constitutionally correct word 'opinion.' Students who know that state legislatures are involved in Article 3 proceedings often fail to distinguish between 'opinion' (advisory, non-binding) and 'consent' (mandatory, blocking). This is a classic scope-extension combined with entity-swap trap applied to constitutional procedure.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 2 and 3 both grant Parliament sweeping territorial powers by simple majority, but they operate on different subjects and have different procedural requirements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 2 covers territories not currently part of India. Parliament can admit or establish them on its own terms through ordinary legislation. Sikkim's 1975 accession used this route.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Article 3 requirement of Presidential reference to the State Legislature applies only when existing states are being reorganised. Article 2 involves territories outside India — there is no existing Indian state whose legislature needs to be consulted.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 3 requires the President to refer the Bill to the State Legislature for its opinion, not for its consent. Parliament can proceed with or without the state's agreement — India's 'indestructible Union' principle in operation.

Value Addition:
• Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 amending the First and Fourth Schedules are not deemed constitutional amendments under Article 368.
• Sikkim's integration: the 35th Amendment (1974) gave Sikkim associate status; the 36th Amendment (1975) made it a full state — Article 2 was used for the initial integration.
• The USA, by contrast, cannot create new states from existing ones without the affected state's consent — a stark federal contrast.

solution.concept_anchor: GST Council vs GST Amendment — majority distinction

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act 2017, which introduced the Goods and Services Tax framework, was passed by Parliament through simple majority as it primarily concerned taxation — a legislative subject.
statement_analysis.reason: The 101st Amendment required the full Article 368 procedure — special majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures — because it altered the constitutional distribution of taxing powers between the Union and States.

statement_analysis.statement: Adding a new language to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution requires passage through the Article 368 special majority procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: Though the Eighth Schedule is an appendix to the Constitution, historical practice (92nd, 71st Amendment Acts) has treated additions to it as constitutional amendments under Article 368, requiring special majority. The judicial position on whether simple majority would suffice is unsettled, but constitutional practice has used Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament can amend the Official Languages Act 1963, which designates Hindi and English as languages for Union official purposes, through ordinary legislation by simple majority.
statement_analysis.reason: The Official Languages Act 1963 is an ordinary statute enacted under Article 344(6). Its amendment requires only simple majority — it is not a constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: The operational procedures and regulations of the GST Council can be altered by simple majority resolutions of Parliament without any constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The GST Council's operational procedures are governed by subordinate regulations and the Council's own rules — these do not require constitutional amendment. Parliament's role in ordinary GST legislation is through simple majority.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who correctly eliminate Statement 1 then also eliminate Statement 2 (thinking 'Schedule changes = simple majority') arrive at three correct statements instead of three.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: GST (101st Amendment) required special majority + state ratification — clearly incorrect. Eliminate.
Evaluate Statement 2: Constitutional practice has consistently used Article 368 for Eighth Schedule additions — correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Official Languages Act 1963 is ordinary legislation — correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: GST Council's operational procedures are by regulation/resolution — no constitutional amendment needed. Correct.
Statements 2, 3, and 4 are correct — 'Only three' — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The master trap: GST is a 'taxation' subject but its constitutional introduction required Article 368's highest tier (special majority + state ratification). Students who classify it as fiscal legislation miss this. The GST Council's procedural rules, conversely, are regulatory — the two must not be conflated.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the ability to distinguish between constitutional amendments (even on economic subjects) and ordinary legislative/regulatory action.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 101st Amendment Act 2017 required Article 368 special majority AND ratification by half the State Legislatures — it modified the constitutional taxation framework (Articles 246A, 269A, 279A), fundamentally altering federal financial relations.
• Statement 2 — Correct: All historical additions to the Eighth Schedule (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali by 92nd Amendment; Sindhi by 71st Amendment) used Article 368 procedure. Constitutional practice treats this as requiring special majority.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Official Languages Act 1963 is a statute under Article 344(6) — Parliament can amend it by simple majority.
• Statement 4 — Correct: GST Council operational rules and resolutions operate below the constitutional level — simple majority suffices.

Three statements (2, 3, 4) are correct — select option (c).

Value Addition:
• The 101st Amendment is the only constitutional amendment requiring state ratification passed in the 21st century (as of 2024).
• Article 344(6) is the source of Parliament's power to enact ordinary language legislation.
• The Eighth Schedule currently lists 22 languages.

solution.concept_anchor: Contingency Fund — constitutional establishment, statutory corpus
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know the Contingency Fund is a constitutional provision assume that any change to it requires constitutional amendment.
elimination_logic: The Contingency Fund of India is established by Article 267(1) — a constitutional provision. Its existence cannot be abolished by simple majority.
However, the corpus (amount) and operational modalities of the Fund are fixed by Parliament through ordinary legislation — the Contingency Fund of India Act 1950.
Changes to the Fund's size are made by amending the Contingency Fund of India Act through simple majority — not through Article 368.
Select option (b): Parliament can alter the corpus of the Contingency Fund through ordinary legislation by simple majority, even though the Fund itself is established by a constitutional article.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The constitutional vs statutory distinction for the Contingency Fund is a recurring exam trap. The Fund's existence is constitutional; its size is statutory. Students who recall 'Contingency Fund is in Article 267' assume any change requires Article 368.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 267 is a good example of a constitutional provision that creates an institution while delegating its operational details to ordinary legislation.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Contingency Fund of India's corpus is not entrenched in the Constitution — it is fixed by the Contingency Fund of India Act 1950, which Parliament can amend by simple majority.
• Option (b) — Correct: Parliament can alter the corpus and operational parameters of the Contingency Fund through ordinary legislation (simple majority) under Article 267's 'by law' authorisation.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: States have their own Contingency Funds under Article 267(2), which can similarly be altered by State Legislatures through ordinary legislation — not by Parliament.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Contingency Fund is placed at the disposal of the President (for the Union) for unforeseen expenditure — it is distinct from the Consolidated Fund and Public Account.

Value Addition:
• The Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266) and the Public Account (Article 266(2)) are similarly established constitutionally but operated through ordinary law.
• Withdrawals from the Contingency Fund are recouped by subsequent parliamentary appropriation.
• State Contingency Funds under Article 267(2) are placed at the disposal of the Governor.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 312 — Rajya Sabha resolution threshold

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 312, the Rajya Sabha can declare the creation of a new All-India Service necessary by passing a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 312(1) requires the Rajya Sabha to support a resolution declaring a new All-India Service necessary by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting. This is the constitutionally specified threshold.

statement_analysis.statement: Once the Rajya Sabha passes the required resolution under Article 312, Parliament must then enact the legislation creating the new All-India Service by a special majority under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: After the Rajya Sabha resolution, Parliament creates the new All-India Service through ordinary legislation by simple majority — not by Article 368 special majority procedure.

statement_analysis.statement: No new All-India Service has been created since the establishment of the Indian Forest Service in 1966.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian Forest Service (IFS) was the last All-India Service created, in 1966. Despite proposals for services like an All-India Education Service, none has been created since.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) misleads students who know 'special majority is involved in Article 312' and apply it to Parliament's legislation rather than the Rajya Sabha resolution.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 312 requires 2/3 of members present and voting in Rajya Sabha — this is correctly stated. Statement 1 is NOT incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Parliament's legislation after the Rajya Sabha resolution is ordinary law by simple majority — NOT special majority. Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: IFS was created in 1966; no new AIS since then — factually correct. Statement 3 is NOT incorrect.
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b). Wait: checking options. Option (b) is '2 only.' Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the classic Article 312 trap — students who know 'Rajya Sabha needs special resolution' conflate the threshold for the resolution with the threshold for the subsequent legislation. The two-step nature of Article 312 (special Rajya Sabha resolution + simple majority law) is one of the most tested procedural details in UPSC Polity questions on simple majority amendments.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 312 creates a federal safeguard through a two-step process for creating new All-India Services.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Rajya Sabha, representing states, must pass a resolution by 2/3 of members present and voting. This threshold reflects the federal concern — states must significantly support the creation of a new service that will be recruited centrally and deployed in states.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Once the Rajya Sabha passes this resolution, Parliament enacts legislation by simple majority to create the service. Article 368's special majority procedure is not involved in the second step.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Indian Forest Service (1966) remains the most recently created All-India Service. Proposals for All-India Education and Health Services have been discussed but not implemented.

Value Addition:
• There are currently three All-India Services: IAS (1946), IPS (1948), IFS (1966).
• The federal safeguard in Article 312 lies in requiring Rajya Sabha (states' representative body) to initiate the process — Lok Sabha alone cannot trigger creation of a new AIS.
• All-India Services officers serve both Union and State governments — hence states' concurrence through Rajya Sabha is built into the process.

solution.concept_anchor: MP salary self-regulation vs judicial salary protection
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Under Article 106, Parliament determines MPs' salaries by law — there is no independent statutory authority equivalent to the UK's IPSA. Parliament votes on its own members' remuneration. A is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts have their salaries fixed in the Second Schedule and charged to the Consolidated Fund — these cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment. R is correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? R describes the judicial salary protection mechanism. This does NOT explain why Parliament self-regulates MPs' salaries — the reason MPs' salaries are self-regulated is Article 106's design, not the existence of judicial salary protection. R is a true fact about a different category of constitutional functionary and does not causally explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two correct but causally unconnected facts about constitutional salary provisions — a classic (b) trap. Students who correctly verify both A and R are true automatically select (a) without examining the causal logic. The careful reader asks: does R explain A? The answer is no — they describe independent constitutional choices.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests whether students can evaluate a causal claim, not just two isolated facts.

**Assertion (A):** Correct. Article 106 provides that Members of Parliament shall be entitled to receive salaries and allowances as determined by Parliament by law. There is no independent regulatory body — Parliament effectively legislates its own members' remuneration, which is subject to the ordinary legislative process (simple majority).

**Reason (R):** Correct. Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts have their salaries specified in the Second Schedule and charged to the Consolidated Fund of India. Their salaries cannot be disadvantageously varied after appointment — a constitutional protection for judicial independence.

**Causal Link:** R does not explain A. The fact that judges have constitutionally entrenched salaries does not cause or explain Parliament's self-regulatory approach to MPs' salaries. These are independent constitutional design choices. A flows from Article 106; R flows from Articles 125 and 221 read with the Second Schedule.

Value Addition:
• The UK's Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (IPSA) — an independent body setting MPs' pay — is often cited as a contrast to India's self-regulatory model.
• Judges' salaries are 'charged' expenditure — they cannot be voted upon during budget debates.
• Parliament's power under Article 106 extends to determining allowances and pension of MPs — all by simple majority.

solution.concept_anchor: Delimitation Commission — statutory finality of orders

statement_analysis.statement: The Delimitation Commission of India is a constitutional body established under Article 82, and its orders carry the force of law primarily because of their constitutional origin.
statement_analysis.reason: The Delimitation Commission is a statutory body created by Parliament under the Delimitation Act (simple majority legislation), not a constitutional body under Article 82. Article 82 merely requires Parliament to readjust constituencies after each census — it is the statutory Delimitation Act that creates the Commission. The orders' finality is also a statutory provision, not a constitutional guarantee.

statement_analysis.statement: The orders of the Delimitation Commission, once published in the Official Gazette, have the force of law and cannot be called in question in any court of law.
statement_analysis.reason: The Delimitation Act contains an explicit provision (Section 10) barring judicial review of the Commission's orders — a unique example of a statutory body whose decisions are immune from court challenge.

solution.strong_distractor: a — wait, evaluating: Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — the answer should be (d). Let me re-check options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d) S1 incorrect S2 correct. Correct answer is (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Delimitation Commission is a statutory body created by the Delimitation Act — not a constitutional body. Its finality is a statutory provision, not a constitutional one. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Delimitation Act explicitly bars judicial challenge to Commission orders — this is factually established and upheld by courts. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 is the plausible fabrication that the Delimitation Commission is a 'constitutional body under Article 82.' Article 82 mandates that Parliament readjust seats after each census — but the Commission itself is created by the Delimitation Act (ordinary law). Students who associate the Commission with Article 82 conflate the constitutional mandate with the statutory mechanism. The Commission's judicial immunity is also often cited as if it derives from the Constitution, when it is actually a statutory provision.
solution.final_explanation:
The Delimitation Commission presents a fascinating constitutional-statutory interface.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Delimitation Commission is not a constitutional body — it is created by Parliament through the Delimitation Act (ordinary legislation by simple majority). Article 82 is the constitutional mandate; the Commission is the statutory mechanism. Its orders' binding nature comes from the statute, not from a constitutional provision.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Section 10 of the Delimitation Act explicitly provides that the Commission's final orders published in the Gazette cannot be challenged in any court. This statutory bar on judicial review is constitutionally unusual and has been upheld by the Supreme Court.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court in Meghraj Kothari v. Delimitation Commission (1966) upheld the non-justiciability of delimitation orders.
• The freeze on seat delimitation (number of seats) was effected through the 42nd Amendment (1976) and extended by the 84th Amendment (2001) — both Article 368 amendments.
• Boundary delimitation (not seat numbers) was carried out by the Delimitation Commission 2002 based on the 2001 census — the next delimitation is expected post-2026 census.

solution.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule vs procedural rules — amendment threshold contrast

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament can alter the quorum required for the conduct of business in either House of Parliament by passing ordinary legislation through simple majority.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100 sets quorum at 1/10th of total membership but Parliament can modify procedural details through ordinary law or rules under Article 118 — these are not entrenched at Article 368 level.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) can be amended by Parliament through the same simple majority procedure used to amend other rules of parliamentary procedure under Article 118.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1985 and is part of the Constitution — any amendment to it requires the Article 368 special majority procedure, not simple majority.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament has the constitutional authority under Article 118 to make rules governing its own procedure and the conduct of business, exercisable by simple majority, without requiring Presidential approval for every rule change.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 118 empowers each House to make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business. These rules are made by simple majority and do not require Presidential approval — the President is consulted only for joint sitting rules under Article 118(3).

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) misleads students who assume that since anti-defection provisions are 'procedural' (governing conduct of members), they must also be simple majority like other procedural rules.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Quorum provisions under Article 100 are in the Constitution but operational details can be adjusted through rules of procedure — simple majority applies. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Tenth Schedule is a constitutional schedule added by the 52nd Amendment — it requires Article 368 special majority to amend, not simple majority. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 118 grants Houses power to make procedural rules by simple majority — Presidential approval not required for routine rules. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap: students who associate 'anti-defection' with 'parliamentary procedure' assume it follows the same amendment route as other procedural rules under Article 118. The Tenth Schedule is a constitutional schedule — its amendment requires special majority, regardless of its subject matter being 'procedural' in nature. This is a classic subject-procedure conflation that UPSC frequently exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary procedure rules (Article 118) and constitutional schedules occupy different legal tiers — even when both concern parliamentary conduct.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Quorum thresholds and procedural details can be modified through the Houses' rule-making power under Article 118 by simple majority.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) is a constitutional schedule inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1985. It is part of the Constitution and requires Article 368 special majority to amend — not the same as ordinary procedural rules.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Each House makes its own rules under Article 118 by simple majority. Presidential approval is required only for rules relating to joint sittings under Article 118(3).

Value Addition:

solution.concept_anchor: Sikkim's admission — Article 2 vs 35th/36th Amendment sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) misleads students who know J&K's reorganisation involved Parliament but assume special majority was used because of J&K's special status under the former Article 370.
elimination_logic: Check option (a): Sikkim was initially admitted through Article 2 route (35th Amendment gave associate status in 1974; 36th Amendment 1975 made it a full state). The pairing of 'Article 2' with Sikkim's integration is historically accurate — correctly matched.

Check option (b): Goa was not admitted under Article 2 — it was already part of India (annexed from Portugal in 1961 by military action; made a UT, then granted statehood in 1987 under Article 3 route through the State of Goa Act 1987). Attributing Goa's statehood to Article 2 is incorrect — Article 2 covers territories 'not part of India,' which was not applicable to Goa by the time of statehood.
Check option (c): J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 — passed by simple majority. This is correctly matched.
Check option (d): Ladakh created as UT without legislature — correctly described. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Goa's statehood is a temporal trap: students conflate Goa's 1961 annexation (which could theoretically involve Article 2 reasoning) with its 1987 statehood (which used Article 3 since it was already a UT). The incorrect pairing sounds authoritative because Goa is indeed a 'special' case of territorial integration.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 2 applies specifically to territories not forming part of India's territory at the time of admission. Once a territory becomes Indian territory (even as a UT), subsequent reorganisation uses Article 3.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Sikkim was not part of India before 1975. The 35th Amendment (1974) gave it associate status; the 36th Amendment (1975) used Article 2 as the constitutional route for full integration.
• Option (b) — NOT correctly matched: Goa's statehood in 1987 was through the State of Goa Act, using the Article 3 route — because Goa had been Indian territory (a UT) since 1961. Article 2 applies to territories outside India, not to existing UTs seeking statehood.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 was ordinary legislation by simple majority, bifurcating J&K into two UTs.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: Ladakh was created as a UT without a legislature — Parliament's plenary power over UT governance allows this through simple majority.

Value Addition:
• Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not constitutional amendments — they do not require Article 368 procedure.
• Goa became a state through the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act 1987.
• Sikkim's integration remains the only post-1950 example of a foreign territory being admitted under Article 2.

solution.concept_anchor: Identifying simple vs special majority — 'by law' clause test
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) misleads students who believe that any change affecting constitutional text or structure must necessarily go through Article 368, regardless of what the article itself says.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a provision that uses the phrase 'Parliament may by law provide' — this is the constitutional signal for ordinary legislation.
A provision that grants Parliament the power to act 'by law' or 'by legislation' is authorising simple majority — it does not route through Article 368.
The impact on federal structure is not the test — several simple majority provisions significantly affect states (Articles 3, 169).
Eliminate (a): A provision explicitly authorising Parliament to act 'by law' is a simple majority provision — not a disguised Article 368 requirement.
Eliminate (c): The federal impact test does not determine majority requirement — the constitutional text does.
Select (b): The correct test is whether the provision itself routes through Article 368 or grants Parliament legislative power through an explicit 'by law' clause.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the assumption that significant federal impact triggers Article 368. In reality, the correct test for identifying whether a provision requires simple or special majority is whether the article itself uses phrases like 'by law,' 'by legislation,' or routes through Article 368's list. Parliament has exercised simple majority power in profoundly federal matters (Article 3 — state reorganisation) without Article 368.
solution.final_explanation:
Identifying whether a constitutional provision requires simple or special majority requires reading the provision itself — not inferring from its subject matter or impact.

**The Test:** If a constitutional article grants Parliament the power to act 'by law' or 'by Parliament by legislation,' it authorises ordinary legislation by simple majority. Article 368 comes into play only when: (i) the provision is in Article 368's explicit list, or (ii) the provision itself says 'notwithstanding Article 368' or specifies a higher threshold.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A 'by law' clause is a definitive signal for simple majority — it does not mean the provision 'could' require Article 368 under some circumstances.
• Option (b) — Correct: The presence of 'by law' or similar language means Parliament acts through ordinary legislation. This is the primary constitutional signal for simple majority action.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Federal impact is not the test. Articles 2, 3, and 169 all affect federal structure but operate through simple majority.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The political sensitivity of a provision does not elevate its constitutional amendment threshold.

Value Addition:
• Key 'by law' articles: Article 11 (citizenship), Article 312 (AIS legislation after RS resolution), Article 138 (SC jurisdiction extension).
• Article 368 itself specifies which provisions require ratification by state legislatures — the highest tier.
• The phrase 'notwithstanding Article 368' or explicit inclusion in Article 368's list is the marker for special majority.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) misleads students who know the 'Eighth Schedule amendment' context and assume that since the Eighth Schedule is 'just a list,' additions to it are simple majority like the Fifth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Identify shared attribute: options (a), (b), (d) involve changes made through ordinary legislation by simple majority — Official Languages Act amendment, Fifth Schedule modification, and Official Languages Act 1963 enactment respectively.

Check option (c): Adding a language to the Eighth Schedule has historically been done through constitutional amendment under Article 368 (71st, 92nd Amendment Acts) requiring special majority — NOT simple majority.
Option (c) is the odd one out — it requires special majority (Article 368) while others require simple majority.
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students assume all Schedules are equal in amendment difficulty. The Eighth Schedule has been treated by Parliament as requiring Article 368, creating a higher amendment bar than the Fifth Schedule. This schedule-specific distinction is a recurring UPSC examination trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Constitutional schedules are not uniformly amendable by simple majority — the amendment route depends on how the Constitution and parliamentary practice treat each schedule.

• Option (a) — Simple majority: The Official Languages Act 1963 is ordinary legislation amendable by Parliament through simple majority under Article 344(6).
• Option (b) — Simple majority: Parliament can modify the Fifth Schedule (including Scheduled Areas) through ordinary legislation — the Fifth Schedule's own provisions permit this.
• Option (c) — Special majority (the odd one out): Every addition to the Eighth Schedule (languages list) has been made through constitutional amendment under Article 368 — 71st Amendment (Sindhi, 1992), 92nd Amendment (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali, 2004). Special majority + in some instances state ratification was used.
• Option (d) — Simple majority: The Original Languages Act 1963's enactment and subsequent amendments are simple majority legislation.

Value Addition:
• The Eighth Schedule currently lists 22 languages; originally it had 14.
• There is ongoing demand for addition of languages like Bhojpuri, Rajasthani, and Tulu to the Eighth Schedule.
• The constitutional basis for the Eighth Schedule is Article 344 — but the Schedule's amendment has been treated as requiring Article 368 by parliamentary convention.

solution.concept_anchor: First Schedule alteration triggers Article 368

statement_analysis.statement: Laws made under Articles 2 and 3 that result in changes to the First and Fourth Schedules of the Constitution are not deemed to be amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 4 explicitly states that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 providing for the amendment of the First and Fourth Schedules shall not be deemed to be amendments for the purposes of Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: When India cedes territory to a foreign country — as in the 100th Amendment involving land exchange with Bangladesh — Parliament can authorise such cession through ordinary legislation without invoking Article 368, because territorial adjustments are administrative in nature.
statement_analysis.reason: The 100th Amendment Act 2015 required Article 368 procedure (special majority + state ratification) because it altered the First Schedule of the Constitution. Territory cession affecting the constitutional territorial description cannot be done by simple majority — it requires Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament's authority to acquire foreign territory for India is derived from executive power (Article 73) and may be subsequently reflected in ordinary legislation, but any change to the First Schedule listing India's territories requires a constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: Territory acquisition is an executive act; its formalisation in the First Schedule requires a constitutional amendment. This distinction — executive act vs constitutional recognition — is important and was illustrated by the 100th Amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: a — wait, checking: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect. The question asks which is NOT correct. Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b) in the multi-statement-incorrect format. Let me check options: (a) 1 only, (b) 2 only, (c) 3 only, (d) 2 and 3 only. Correct answer is (b).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 4 explicitly provides this — laws under Articles 2 and 3 altering the First and Fourth Schedules are not Article 368 amendments. Statement 1 is correct (NOT incorrect).

Evaluate Statement 2: The 100th Amendment required Article 368 — special majority + state ratification. Territory cession affecting the First Schedule cannot be simple majority. Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Territory acquisition is an executive act; First Schedule alteration needs constitutional amendment. Statement 3 is correct (NOT incorrect).
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial truth — territorial adjustments can involve executive and legislative action. But the specific claim that cession affecting the First Schedule can be done by 'ordinary legislation' is incorrect. The 100th Amendment is the direct counterexample. Students who generalise 'territorial changes = simple majority' from the Article 3 reorganisation context incorrectly apply the same rule to First Schedule cession.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional treatment of territorial changes distinguishes between internal reorganisation (Articles 2 and 3) and changes to India's international borders affecting the First Schedule.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 4 carves out laws under Articles 2 and 3 from the Article 368 definition of 'amendment.' This means Parliament can reorganise states and admit new ones through simple majority without it being a constitutional amendment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 100th Amendment Act 2015 (Bangladesh land boundary) required Article 368 procedure — special majority in both Houses and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures — because it altered the First Schedule's territorial description. This cannot be done by ordinary legislation.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Territory acquisition rests with executive power under Article 73 (foreign relations); its constitutional recognition through First Schedule alteration requires Article 368.

Value Addition:
• Article 4 is the provision that makes Articles 2 and 3 laws non-amendments — a crucial exam fact.
• The 100th Amendment is unique as the only post-independence amendment involving international border cession requiring state ratification.
• India acquired Berubari Union territory but ceded it to Pakistan — the Berubari Reference (1960) established that territory cession requires constitutional amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: Fifth vs Sixth Schedule — states and governance features
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) traps students who know 'Mizoram is Sixth Schedule' but swap Mizoram with Manipur or confuse the President's power (Fifth Schedule) with Governor's power.
elimination_logic: Match A (Autonomous District Councils): Autonomous District Councils are the governance mechanism under the Sixth Schedule — match with 4.
Match B (Modification of Scheduled Areas by Presidential order): The Fifth Schedule Para 6 vests this power in the President — match with 2.
Match C (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — applicability): The Sixth Schedule applies to these four states — match with 3.
Match D (PESA Act 1996): PESA extends Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas — match with 1.
Correct: A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1 — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic trap swaps the Sixth Schedule's applicability (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) with incorrect state combinations. Students who partially know the Sixth Schedule states may confuse Mizoram with Manipur or include Arunachal Pradesh. Beginning the matching from the clearest anchor (Autonomous District Councils = Sixth Schedule) is the exam strategy.
solution.final_explanation:
The Fifth and Sixth Schedules have distinct governance features, geographic applicability, and institutional structures.

**Correct Matches:**
• A (Autonomous District Councils) — 4: The Sixth Schedule establishes Autonomous District Councils in the designated tribal areas of northeastern states. These councils have quasi-legislative, executive, and judicial powers.
• B (Presidential order to modify Scheduled Areas) — 2: Para 6 of the Fifth Schedule vests the power to increase, decrease, or alter the boundaries of Scheduled Areas in the President through public notification.
• C (Applicability to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) — 3: The Sixth Schedule applies to these four states. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, and Manipur are NOT under the Sixth Schedule.
• D (PESA Act 1996) — 1: The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 extends the Panchayati Raj framework (73rd Amendment) to Fifth Schedule areas with tribal-specific modifications. It is ordinary legislation.

Value Addition:
• The Fifth Schedule has no analogue to District Councils — tribal governance in Fifth Schedule areas is through ordinary Panchayati Raj institutions (with PESA modifications).
• Sixth Schedule courts (Village Courts) can try certain offences — a quasi-judicial function absent in Fifth Schedule areas.
• Governors have a special role in Fifth Schedule areas (tribal advisory councils) — distinct from their ordinary role.

solution.concept_anchor: Simple majority — definition as majority of members present and voting
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'majority of total membership' sounds like the ordinary meaning of 'majority' and students who have not precisely studied the distinction will confuse 'simple majority' with 'absolute majority.'
elimination_logic: Simple majority is technically defined as a majority of members present and voting — it does not count absentees.
Absolute majority is a majority of total membership of the House — this is the definition in option (b).
Special majority under Article 368 requires 2/3 of members present and voting AND majority of total membership — a double condition.
The blank describing simple majority must be filled with 'majority of members present and voting' — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Simple majority is often confused with absolute majority in examination conditions. The technical definition ('present and voting') versus the intuitive reading ('total membership') is the trap. Article 100 is the source of the simple majority definition.
solution.final_explanation:
Precision in majority definitions is essential for UPSC Polity questions on the amendment procedure.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: '2/3 of members present and voting' is the threshold for the Rajya Sabha's special resolution under Article 312 or part of the Article 368 special majority requirement — not simple majority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'Majority of the total membership of the House' is the definition of absolute majority — used in contexts like votes of no confidence (Article 75) and Article 169 State Assembly resolutions.
• Option (c) — Correct: Simple majority means a majority of members present and voting in the House (quorum being present). This is the standard for ordinary legislation and is the default for parliamentary decision-making.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: '3/4 of members present and voting' is not a standard constitutional majority threshold in India.

Value Addition:
• Article 100(1): All questions in either House are decided by a majority of members present and voting (simple majority) — the default constitutional rule.
• Special majority under Article 368: 2/3 of members present and voting (in each House) AND majority of total membership of each House — both conditions must be met simultaneously.
• Effective majority: majority of the effective strength of the House (excluding vacancies) — used in some specific contexts.
